value.overview: The Lineated Woodpecker (Dryocopus lineatus) is a large Neotropical woodpecker found from Mexico through Central and South America. It has mostly black plumage, a prominent red crest, pale lines on the face and shoulders, and a pale, barred underside. It is often seen on tree trunks and large limbs, where it searches for insects and excavates nest cavities. The species is adaptable and commonly uses forest edges, open woodland, and mature secondary habitats.
value.classification: The Lineated Woodpecker belongs to the woodpecker family Picidae and the order Piciformes. It is one of several large Dryocopus woodpeckers in the tropical Americas.
value.identification: This is a large, powerful woodpecker with black upperparts, a red crest, pale facial stripes, and white or buff lines along the sides of the back. The underparts are pale buff to whitish and heavily marked with black streaks and bars. Males have more red on the forehead and facial markings, while females have a darker forehead and malar stripe. The bill is pale in northern Costa Rica and darker farther south. Its loud calls, strong drumming, and upright trunk-climbing posture are distinctive.
value.rangeHabitat: The Lineated Woodpecker ranges from Mexico south through Central America into much of South America, including parts of the Guianas, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Paraguay, and Argentina. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, occurring from sea level through the lowlands of both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes and locally reaching about 1,100 meters. It uses forest edges, gallery forest, older secondary woodland, shaded gardens, scattered pasture trees, and other partly open habitats, but is less frequent in dense, very wet forest.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and generally nonmigratory throughout its range. Individuals may move locally in response to food availability and habitat conditions, but regular seasonal migration is not known.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding is reported mainly from January through May. The species excavates a nest cavity in a tree, usually between about 3 and 30 meters above the ground. A typical clutch contains three or four eggs. Both members of a pair participate in defending a territory and caring for young. Nest trees may be standing dead trees or living trees with suitable decayed wood, and abandoned cavities can later provide shelter or nesting sites for other wildlife.
value.dietFeeding: The Lineated Woodpecker feeds mainly on ants, beetle larvae, other insects, and their eggs or pupae found beneath bark or inside wood. It also takes some fruits and may visit flowering or fruiting trees. The bird climbs trunks and large branches, probing and hammering with its heavy bill. Its long, bristled tongue helps extract prey from crevices and cavities, while forceful excavation opens deeper sections of rotten wood.
value.behavior: Lineated Woodpeckers are usually solitary or found in pairs, and pairs may remain associated throughout the year. They forage deliberately on trunks, limbs, dead branches, and exposed wood, often producing loud blows while excavating. Individuals roost separately in tree holes. Their large nest cavities are ecologically important because they may be reused by smaller birds, mammals, reptiles, and insects after the woodpeckers leave.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not considered to indicate a major conservation decline, although local abundance can vary with habitat loss and forest degradation.
